toc.title: Irritation is evidence of fight activation
If your body says move, move
Validate, normalize, and permit the fight activation too
What the story tells you about safety
Frustrated about shutdown, and a little anxious
"How can I make the energy last?"

blocks.p: You're trying to self-regulate out of shutdown and work your way up the Polyvagal ladder, but you keep stumbling onto frustration, irritation, and maybe even anger. Is this expected, a normal part of the process? Or is it an obstacle and a red flag? Let's look at what's happening within you and what you can do about it.

I got a really great question from a member of my community who has been working through my Shutdown to Stillness course, and I think it relates to a lot of people who are working their way out of shutdown. I'll share it, and then share my thoughts. I've made up a name for this person: Teagan. This is my general take, not specific life advice for Teagan or anybody else, but I'll get as specific as I can.

q: I'm finding it hard to give permission to my shutdown state. I've moved from resistance and experienced acceptance and some stillness. But now I feel that I can only tolerate it.

Yesterday I used the idea of imagery, seeing/feeling my shutdown as a big black cloak. This led to me getting irritated and I got up, moved around, and started saying, "Get off me" and "Leave me alone." I stayed grounded and felt connected. Energy definitely came back, but only for about 10 minutes. Shutdown returned, although not as heavy.

blocks.p: Permitting any defensive state is a challenge, no matter what your stuck defensive state is. And yet giving permission is extremely important, because if you don't permit it to be there, how can you mindfully experience it, feel it, and then self-regulate out of that stuck defensive state?

What I'm hearing is that Teagan is slowly coming out of shutdown into stillness. She's had some acceptance. I'm assuming that means something like validation: it's real, it's here, and I'm not going to minimize it or deny it anymore. I have this experience of shutdown, like sadness or heaviness or feeling hopeless. And maybe even some stillness already, which is a good sign.

We don't want to go all the way into shutdown all at once. A deep dive into stuck shutdown is potentially a lot. So there's a gentler way of permitting shutdown that uses imagery, and that's what Teagan did. Her shutdown looked like a big black cloak, something heavy just hanging on her.

blocks.h: Irritation is evidence of fight activation

blocks.p: This led to Teagan getting irritated. Does that mean the imagery made her irritated? No. It means that successfully permitting shutdown in this way led to irritation.
The way I interpret this, irritation is a good indication of fight activation. No matter what the impetus is, the fact that there's fight activation is a pretty good sign of self-regulation.

In Shutdown to Stillness, the goal is not to go into fight activation, although it could happen. The goal is stillness. Stillness is a combination of shutdown plus safety. We're trying to get a really good amount of safety active along with permitting shutdown. Combining those two results in stillness, which typically feels like relaxation, curiosity, and maybe even interest in our inner world. At a really intense level, maybe awe.

So irritation, or frustration, or maybe even anger, doesn't mean "this doesn't work, and therefore I'm angry." It's "oh, there's anger within me in the present moment. That's a good indication that I'm no longer in shutdown, or less in shutdown, and now I've worked my way up the Polyvagal ladder into my sympathetic flight or fight state," and specifically fight.
As we come out of shutdown, the first step up the Polyvagal ladder is fight. It goes shutdown, then fight, flight, and then safety.

We have to work our way out of shutdown in the reverse order of how we got there. We went into shutdown because we could not be safe, could not run away, could not fight, whatever the context of our life was. So to come out of a stuck shutdown state, we go through the reverse order: shutdown, fight, flight, and then back into safety.
Deb Dana put it this way when I interviewed her:

q: To begin to leave dorsal, you have to travel through sympathetic… we have to have our energy used in an organized way and often in connection with somebody else.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: So it's very common, and quite predictable, that as we come out of a stuck shutdown we experience something that comes from fight activation. Typically that's irritation. A mild irritation could linger. People might notice they're more snappy, even toward people they care about. They snap back. They're not really filtering their comments very much. It's not rage. Rage would come from freeze. Irritability is very, very common, and so is frustration: "I'm tired of this. I want to change. I want to get out of this stuck state."

Frustration comes from emerging fight activation. It's potentially a very, very good sign. When I hear my clients in shutdown tell me they're feeling frustration, I get excited, because here we go. Now we have some sympathetic activation coming back into your system. If we can mindfully be with that, the next step of self-regulation can unfold.

blocks.h: If your body says move, move

blocks.p: Teagan got irritated, then got up and moved around. That's really good. When we notice mobility coming back into our system, when the sympathetic system is coming back on, getting up and moving around is a very good idea. That might be a walk around the block. It might be pushups. It might be pulling on your hands and flexing your back muscles, your chest muscles, or your biceps. Movement is great. As we feel sympathetic activation, if our body is saying move, get moving. It sounds like that's what Teagan's body was telling her: hey, it's time to get going.
This isn't stillness. This is mobility, and that's great. The goal of the course is more and more stillness, but sympathetic activation could emerge, and that's okay.

blocks.h: Validate, normalize, and permit the fight activation too

blocks.p: Then Teagan started saying, "Get off me" and "Leave me alone." Story follows state, as Deb Dana says: the thoughts in our brain change depending on the dominant state of our body. "Get off me" and "leave me alone" don't sound like shutdown to me. They sound like fight activation, sympathetic activation. It sounds almost like empowerment: I'm tired of this, I'm moving forward, I'm changing.

But to me it doesn't indicate a mindful experiencing of fight activation. And that's okay. It's normal to come out of shutdown and have fight activation without expecting it, so it just feels like frustration: "Ah, forget this stuff. I'm giving up." No matter what comes up, we do the same process:

ol: Validate it. Recognize it for what it is.
Normalize it. Does it make sense that I feel fight activation right now? Yes. That means I'm coming out of shutdown. It's an expected response.
Permit it. Can I permit my fight activation to be here? Can I let myself feel irritated? Can I let myself feel frustrated?

blocks.p: If you can give it permission to be there, you can mindfully experience that as well, and that can unfold the next step of self-regulation.

blocks.h: What the story tells you about safety

blocks.p: The flavor of "get off me, leave me alone" leans toward the defensive side. There's rejection in it: I don't want this experience. That tells me we're probably losing some access to safety, and with it some access to compassion and patience, and to being in the present moment with all of our experiences, with curiosity.

I don't blame Teagan or anybody else for having this thought. It's not a failure, and I'm not saying you're doing it wrong. Ideally, if we have enough access to our safety state through the process of self-regulation, the thoughts will lean toward safety, toward more self-compassion. Instead of "get off me, leave me alone," it might be: "I'm doing it. There's fight activation coming up within me. I can't believe I'm able to do this." Or, "My wonderful body. Yay." Or, "I'm getting to the next step of connecting to myself, deeper in the present moment." There will be more hope, more connection. The thoughts are different when there's more safety in the system. With less safety, there's more rejection of what's happening within.

Nobody likes the shutdown experience. It's not pleasurable, and I don't blame anybody for that. But even though we don't like it, we can still have compassion, empathy, and understanding for it, for the experiences of our life, and for our stuck defensive state.

Teagan also said she stayed grounded and felt connected. That's a really good sign. So it's not all or nothing. There's definitely some defense there, and there's still some safety present to feel grounded and connected, probably a good enough balance to keep going. I'd lean toward reconnecting to the present-moment experience in your body with compassion, as much as you can. And if your goal is to keep self-regulating up the Polyvagal ladder, validate, normalize, and give permission to the fight activation as it comes up.

Teagan's energy came back for about 10 minutes, then shutdown returned, although not as heavy. That's pretty expected. There's no hard and fast rule about the 10 minutes. It is what it is. But shutdown returning, not as heavy, is a pretty good sign that we're working our way out of shutdown.

It's not all or nothing, and it's not all at once. We work our way out of defensive states a little bit at a time. We'll likely go back into that defensive state, even as a dominant state, but not as intensely. Things just get better and feel better over time, little by little. There's more mobility coming back into the system, and less shutdown.

I'd worry less about how much time it lasts, and more about how much permission you're giving it to be there. If you can give your fight activation permission to be present for two minutes, really feeling it and owning it with compassion, that's probably better than struggling to hold on to it for 10 minutes. Feel it, validate it, normalize it, give it permission to be there. Even if it's only two minutes, that's a huge win in my book.
Teagan asked, "It feels like I went from shutdown straight to fight without the stillness phase. Does this matter? Any insights as to why this may have happened?"

No, you had the stillness phase. Being able to sit still and look inward, being able to use imagery and allow there to be an image for the shutdown experience: all of that comes from stillness. You had so much anchoring in your safety state, into stillness with shutdown, that you were actually able to allow the next step of self-regulation.

Your dominant shutdown state plus a present-moment safety state: those combine to create stillness. If you can immobilize and be okay with it, you are in stillness. We just want access to that to grow. The fact that you're showing up, sitting down, and thinking critically means you already have some stillness. We just want to draw that out, get deeper into it, and notice the experience of stillness mindfully. It sounds like Teagan has a pretty good amount of stillness already, so much so that her body was saying, "Cool, now we're ready for some more self-regulation."

blocks.h: Frustrated about shutdown, and a little anxious

blocks.p: Teagan wrote, "I can still feel that I'm frustrated with being in shutdown as I write this, but also a little anxious about this too."

Let's focus on the frustration. No matter what you're frustrated about, frustration is evidence of fight activation, of mobility. The brain is going to come up with an explanation. It'll say, "I'm frustrated about my shutdown," or "I'm frustrated about that thing at work." Whatever the about is, your body is in a state of mobilization. That is fantastic. It's a much different experience than shutdown.

A little anxious could be some flight activation as well. I like how she said "a little." It's emerging, but the frustration, the fight activation, is more dominant. That tells me shutdown might be receding, fight activation is increasing, and there's even a little flight activation coming along with it. Remember the Polyvagal ladder: shutdown, to fight, to flight.

blocks.h: "How can I make the energy last?"

blocks.p: Teagan asked, "How can I sustain any returning energy for more than 10 minutes?"

I wouldn't try to. I wouldn't try to make it last a certain amount of time, and I wouldn't try to limit it. Ideally, we're with it while it's there, and the body will do what it needs to do. If you can feel it mindfully, be with that activation in your body. Maybe you feel it in your breathing, in your chest, or you feel your muscles starting to tense up. That tells you something is happening within you. If you can be with that, maybe use a fidget to release it, or pull on your hands, or push on a wall, or just go for a walk. Whatever feels right.

If you can be with that emerging mobility, I personally don't care how long it lasts. Being with it gives it permission to stay. The next time you try your self-regulation practices, you're probably going to be more successful. It'll probably have an easier time coming back, and the dominant shutdown will continue to soften and recede in intensity.

Worrying about whether you're doing it right, or whether it's the right amount of time, comes from evaluation, and evaluation comes more from defensive activation. Don't worry about doing it right or wrong. Do the best you can to be with it.

She also asked, "Is it unrealistic to expect more, having been shut down for so long?" Yeah, probably. The intensity of it, the flavor of it, how long it hangs out in your system: as you keep tapping into mobility, it's going to shift. Right now it might be frustration. Then you have a win and you feel more self-compassion, and the next day it feels like motivation. Two weeks from now it might feel like creativity. Two weeks after that it might feel like, "Oh, I'm ready to apply to that new job." It might feel like productivity, or "I'm ready to go exercise." It changes. Whatever it is, be with it as it is in the present moment as best you can.

Having been stuck in shutdown for so long, the returning activation probably won't be super intense, especially if you're focusing on safety as central to self-regulation, which I highly recommend. If you focus on safety, the returning defensive activation will be smaller. It'll feel like irritability. It won't feel like, "Oh my god, I'm angry out of nowhere." Irritability is something you can notice and totally sit with. You can validate it, normalize it, and permit it to be there.
Teagan's final question: "Should I focus on harnessing this frustration with shutdown, using my safety anchors, or return to focusing on permission and stillness?"

I recommend focusing on stillness. It sounds like there's some emerging fight activation, and when you focus on settling into stillness through safety anchors, your body will take care of the rest. You'll feel that activation come up within you, just like you did here.

The focus is what's happening in the present moment. What's happening inside of me? Can I connect to the present moment externally? Can I use my senses mindfully, and what does it feel like to do that? All of that requires a really good amount of stillness, which requires safety. So:

ol: Keep doing your safety anchors practice, and make sure you're in a passive safety environment.
Mindfully experience what it's like to be in your safety state.
Then ask, "Hey, what's it like to be in shutdown?" and let that be there. When you permit it, it connects with safety, and that brings you into stillness.
From stillness, notice what that's like.

blocks.p: And all of a sudden, we're off to the races. You might notice some emerging fight activation coming back up within you, more mobility. If you can notice more mobility and act on it, now you're at that next step of self-regulation.
Teagan, it sounds like you're doing a really good job.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.
